case_study_insert.main_stem: Trailmark Northern Logistics (TNL) is a private limited company in the road freight and parcel logistics sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Freya Marsh, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TNL plans to invest $720,000 in a fleet of GPS-tracked electric delivery vans and a depot charging hub, financed by a $450,000 five-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8 a unit and a selling price of $20, and currently produces 60,000 units a year. TNL also faces driver absenteeism of 8% and a rising parcel-damage rate at the depot, and aims to cut delivery emissions while protecting its supermarket contracts.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: TNL handled 15,000 parcels last quarter at a damage rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 19 per month, and average order fulfilment is 2.6 days. A survey of 450 business clients found that 68% value real-time GPS tracking and 55% would pay $1.50 more for carbon-neutral delivery. A training audit shows 18 of 60 drivers are not yet certified on the electric vans; an external certification course costs $750 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Trailmark Northern Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.80 to $14.60 per hour from April 2027. (3) Diesel and electric-vehicle battery input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while demand for low-emission logistics grew 4.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: TNL is funding part of its electric-van expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for TNL of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or fixed repayments, so TNL keeps the cash that would otherwise service the $450,000 five-year bank loan. That cash can absorb fixed costs of $300,000 a year and fund the running of the new $720,000 electric-van fleet while driver absenteeism of 8% is still lifting costs. Every dollar saved in interest can be spent on the depot charging hub or on reducing the 2.4% parcel-damage rate, helping TNL protect its supermarket contracts without raising the $20 selling price.

Point 2: Using $270,000 retained profit leaves control with Freya Marsh's management team instead of a lender, so no bank can impose conditions on how the GPS-tracked vans or the charging hub are operated. It also avoids pledging company assets when the 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate still need attention, giving the 60-strong workforce room to stabilise service before taking on more debt. The survey evidence that 68% of clients value GPS tracking and 55% would pay $1.50 more shows where internally saved cash can be reinvested, rather than being paid to a bank as interest that competes directly with the $300,000 fixed costs and the cost of the fleet expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to TNL and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: TNL is promoting its new low-emission van fleet. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio sponsorship, or targeted social media and van-livery promotion. Which should TNL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A TV advert would build awareness of TNL's low-emission van fleet across the whole country very quickly, which could help win new supermarket contracts. However, airtime and production costs are very high for a 60-employee logistics firm already servicing a $450,000 loan and investing $720,000, and most viewers do not buy freight or parcel services. Much of the spend would be wasted, and television cannot demonstrate the GPS tracking that 68% of surveyed clients value.

Regional radio sponsorship: Sponsorship of local radio is much cheaper and reaches TNL's regional catchment where its 15,000 quarterly parcels are collected, so it suits a time-sensitive message about a new electric fleet. Its weakness is narrow reach: radio listeners are not necessarily the 450 business clients in the survey, and a 2.4% parcel-damage rate is better addressed by showing service quality than by buying airtime.

Targeted social media and van-livery promotion: Posts aimed at logistics managers, combined with branding on the GPS-tracked vans themselves, reach exactly the buyers who place freight contracts and can demonstrate the tracking and lower emissions. This is low cost per contact, measurable, and reinforces the 55% who would pay $1.50 more for greener delivery; it also lets TNL answer complaints directly and show how the charging hub cuts damage and downtime.

Recommendation: TNL should choose targeted social media and van livery. It reaches the precise decision-makers, costs far less than television, and works nationally unlike local radio. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 60-person operator funding a $450,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow for clients spread across supermarket supply chains. Social media lacks television's mass reach, so TNL should support it with a small regional radio top-up during the launch weeks only.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TNL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of TNL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: TNL's driver absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for TNL of using autocratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve reliability.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Freya Marsh set clear, uniform delivery and vehicle-check procedures for all 60 drivers, so everyone follows the same routine regardless of the 8% absenteeism rate. In a hierarchical structure, instructions pass down a defined chain of command, which reduces confusion when drivers are swapped between routes at short notice and helps hold the 2.4% parcel-damage rate steady.

Point 2: Quick, central decisions speed up responses to problems on the new $720,000 electric-van fleet: managers can immediately reassign routes or order a replacement van when charging or breakdown issues arise, protecting the 15,000 quarterly parcels and the 2.6-day fulfilment target. Clear expectations also make it easier to identify who needs the $750 certification course, so the 18 uncertified drivers are trained in a controlled way. This decisiveness suits an operation servicing a $450,000 loan, where delay costs money; the 68% of clients valuing GPS tracking can be assured that standards are enforced consistently. Autocratic leadership is most effective here because the work is rule-based and time-critical, allowing TNL to stabilise reliability before considering more participative methods.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TNL's absenteeism, damage rate and fleet investment.

questions.question_text: TNL wants to cut its 8% absenteeism and 2.4% parcel-damage rate. Consider a performance-related bonus or job enrichment through team working. Which should TNL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: Paying drivers for low damage and full attendance could motivate the 60 staff to reduce the 8% absenteeism rate and the 2.4% parcel-damage rate, and it is easy to measure against the 15,000 quarterly parcels. However, the insert gives no bonus cost, so its expense cannot be quantified; it would add to fixed costs of $300,000 a year at a time when TNL is servicing a $450,000 loan and funding a $720,000 fleet. A bonus also rewards outcomes after the event and does not change the routine that causes damage.

Job enrichment through team working: Giving drivers varied routes, shared responsibility for vehicle checks and a say in depot layout makes the work less repetitive and uses their local knowledge, which can cut the 2.4% damage rate at source. Team checks can also spot the faults behind the 34 monthly complaints, and shared ownership can reduce the 8% absenteeism by raising commitment. The drawback is the time needed to organise teams in a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership, and results may be slower than a bonus.

Decision: TNL should choose job enrichment through team working. It addresses the causes of absenteeism and damage rather than paying around them, costs little compared with a bonus, and fits the 18 drivers needing $750 certification by pairing them with experienced colleagues. The bonus is rejected as an expensive short-term payment whose size is unstated and which does not change working methods, though a small bonus could be added later once teams are established. With no stated bonus rate, the comparison is qualitative: team working changes how the 60 drivers work, while a bonus only rewards them after damage has occurred.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job enrichment with limited application to TNL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of TNL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering absenteeism, damage, cost and motivation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TNL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($20 − $8) = $300,000 ÷ $12 = 25,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 25,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20 − $8 = $12. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TNL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 25,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 60,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 35,000 units, so managers can see how far demand could fall before the $720,000 van fleet stops covering costs.
2. Use the $12 contribution per unit to test pricing: a $1 cut to $19 leaves $11 contribution, requiring about 27,273 units (300,000 ÷ 11) to cover the $300,000 fixed costs, which helps judge whether the 55% willing to pay $1.50 more should instead be offered a discount.
3. Average total cost is $13.00 a unit ($300,000 ÷ 60,000 = $5.00 plus $8), below the $20 price, leaving room to absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and battery costs without an immediate price increase.
4. Labour productivity is 1,000 units per worker (60,000 ÷ 60), a benchmark for checking whether the $750 driver certification and team working lift output while the 8% absenteeism persists.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 25,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 35,000 units against 60,000 output; a $1 price cut leaving $11 contribution and about 27,273 units needed; average total cost of $13.00 against the $20 price; labour productivity of 1,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TNL's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has TNL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.5%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 900, cost of sales 540, gross profit 360; operating profit 135; capital employed 900. 2025 revenue 1,080, cost of sales 594, gross profit 486; operating profit 189; capital employed 1,080. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 360 ÷ 900 and 486 ÷ 1,080. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 135 ÷ 900 and 189 ÷ 1,080. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 135 ÷ 900 and 189 ÷ 1,080.

Evaluation: Every measure is higher in 2025. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 40.0% to 45.0% because revenue grew by 180 while cost of sales rose by only 54, so the electric-fleet operation is becoming more efficient. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,080 of capital employed improved, which matters because TNL must service a $450,000 loan while funding a $720,000 expansion. The 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate remain risks, but they have not prevented stronger profitability. Interest payable of 24 in 2025 is modest beside operating profit of 189, so financing costs are not eroding the gain.

Conclusion: TNL's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, with revenue growing much faster than cost of sales. Management should use the stronger margins to fund driver certification and damage reduction so that absenteeism does not reverse the improvement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether TNL improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TNL of introducing GPS-tracked electric vans with a depot charging hub.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 450 business clients found that 68% value real-time GPS tracking and 55% would pay $1.50 more for carbon-neutral delivery, so the new vans can win contracts and add contribution above the $8 variable cost per unit. Better tracking also lets managers tackle the 2.4% parcel-damage rate and the 19 remaining monthly complaints, protecting the $20 selling price and the 60,000-unit output.

Disadvantage: The $720,000 fleet and charging hub add to the capital TNL must finance with a $450,000 loan, and charging downtime could reduce the 15,000 parcels handled each quarter if recharging is not managed. The insert gives no electricity or maintenance cost, so the exact running-cost saving cannot be calculated; only a qualitative judgement is possible. The 8% absenteeism rate may also mean drivers are not always available to charge and check the vans, so the 18 uncertified drivers need their $750 course before the fleet is fully used. The advantage depends on the 55% premium being accepted across all contracts, not just in the survey.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TNL's survey, damage rate and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase to $14.60 and the 9.5% rise in diesel and battery costs will affect TNL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If TNL's $450,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year, shown as 0.0075 × $450,000. That is small against $300,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is zero. Higher rates may still slow the 4.2% growth in low-emission logistics demand.

Minimum wage increase (5.8% to $14.60 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage cost cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 60,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,000 units per worker. If that holds, the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 8% absenteeism and 2.4% damage rate reduce effective output, unit labour costs rise and the $12 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified here.

Input-cost inflation (9.5%): The $8 variable cost is not split into components, so an explicit upper bound is 9.5% × $8 = $0.76 per unit. Across 60,000 units that is 60,000 × $0.76 = $45,600 a year. Even a smaller rise cuts contribution from $12 toward about $11.24 and pushes the break-even output above 25,000 units.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and battery costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 60,000 units and directly erodes the $12 contribution that must cover $300,000 fixed costs and service the $450,000 loan, whereas the interest rise is about $3,375 and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. TNL can recover part of it through the $1.50 premium that 55% of clients accept.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TNL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TNL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
